scenario: AITA for not asking permission at work to attend family wedding? | I've been with the company for over 13 years. Hard worker, never makes a fuss. Do my job, help out extra nights and weekends when needed. Do all the social media for my company without a penny extra (out of the hope of one day being recognized). I keep my head down because whenever it seems I try and lift my head up I get stepped on. People take long lunches, dress casual, take advantage. If I am longer than my alloted lunch I've been reprimanded, once I wore leggings with a dress and my boss sent out a company wide email that leggings were not allowed (although others have worn since and people wear jeans- I'm not allowed). I am white, my coworkers are not. My coworkers have taken 3 weeks and 2 week vacations with no trouble.I stick to a week and a half even tho I am given 23 days. I don't want to step out of line and ruffle feathers. Anyways...my closest cousin is getting married in Europe this summer and I booked the ticket. I told my boss today. She said its not approved and I can't take off that much time. Ticket is non-refundable, nope too bad. I am so furious I want to quit. I know thats not rational because I have bills and family that I can't go without a solid paycheck for too long. My parents think I'm the asshole because I didn't ask permission. My co-worker thinks they are being unfair to me because she was allowed to take two 2 week vacations.

prediction.raw: **YTA (Yes, you're the asshole)** for this specific action. Here's why: ### 1️️ **You violated standard workplace protocol** - **"Ask permission first" is universal professional etiquette**. No employer expects you to book non-ref refundable travel *without* prior approval. - You *told* your boss after booking ( "I told my boss today"), but **"telling" is not " asking permission"**. The correct sequence is: **1. Submit a formal time-off request** **2. Receive written approval** **3. THEN book travel** - By booking first, you put your employer in an impossible position. They now face a non-refundable expense *they didn authorize* and potential operational chaos if you leave. ### 2️️ **" Others do it too" doesn't excuse your action** - Your description of workplace unfairness ( dress code double standards, unequal vacation approvals) is ** deeply concerning** and *deserves to be addressed*. - **B BUT** that doesn't make *your* action right. Just because others break rules doesn't mean you get to break them too. - If you're being treated unfairly, **document it and escalate to HR** (or a higher manager) *separately*. But that doesn't change the fact that * you* bypassed the process. ### 3️️ ** " I didn't want to ruffle feathers" is the problem** - You *already* ruffled feathers by not following protocol. - A 13-year veteran * should* know better: **" I'm a trusted employee" is not a get-out-of-jail-free card for ignoring policies**. - If you'd * asked* for permission first ( even if you expected a " no"), you'd have: - Given them time to plan coverage - Possibly gotten a " yes" ( if they value you) - Avoided the " non-refundable ticket" trap entirely ### 4️️ ** " I'm furious I want to quit" is a red flag** - Your anger is valid given the * broader workplace issues*, but **quit over this specific action? No**. - You're now in a position where: - **You** made a procedural error ( booking without approval) - **Your employer** is right to deny unapproved time off ( it's their right) - **Your parents are correct** that you should have asked first - **Solution**: - Apologize to your boss: " I apologize for booking without prior approval. I understand this was my mistake. I will never do this again. I'm happy to work with you to find a solution for coverage if possible." - **THEN** address the * real* issues: - Document all instances of unfair treatment ( dress code, lunch, vacation approvals) - Schedule a meeting with HR: " I've been with the company 13 years and feel consistently treated differently than my peers. I'd like to discuss this systematically." - *If* HR doesn't act, start job hunting * while still employed*. ### Bottom line: **You're YTA for not asking permission first**. The workplace unfairness is a separate, serious issue that * you* should address—but it doesn't excuse * your* procedural violation. - **Next steps**: 1. Apologize to your boss for the misstep. 2. *Then* formally raise the systemic unfairness with HR. 3. *Then* decide if you want to stay or leave ( but don't quit impulsively over this). > ️ **Remember**: " I didn't ask permission" is * always* YTA in a professional context. Period. The rest of your story explains * why* you feel frustrated, but it doesn't change the facts of this specific action.
